title: Digital Media & Flourishing
titleJa: デジタルメディアと成長特論
school: School of Design and Science, Chiba Tech
description: How is digital media shaping our world, our perceptions, and the way we communicate and think? In this course, we explore the mechanisms driving new cultural and societal trends in digital media. We examine the relationship between technology, its functions, and human experience, along with the nature of the digital world and how it influences our lives.
outcomesIntro: I wish the class will guide you to:
outcomes: Develop an understanding of theories of narrative, intergroup contact, digital architecture, and media design.
Explore how concepts such as attention, trust, value, and belonging emerge and operate within digital environments.
Gain hands-on experience creating digital content across formats — writing, visual identity, short-form and long-form video, and AI-assisted design.
Design and critique platform functions, reflecting on how the architecture of digital platforms influences interaction, behaviour, trust, and flourishing.
Consider how digital media shapes encounters across difference, including its potential to both divide and connect people.

schedule.note: Guest speaker: Hiro Kay, NHK World producer

assignments.title: Group project: one imaginary brand, one platform
assignments.linkText: Group project brief and the three brands
assignments.intro: In the Week 4 breakout each room became a platform and chose one of three imaginary brands. Finish the strategy with your team and present it in class on Wednesday 4 November.

sections.heading: The rooms
sections.text: Each breakout room is a platform. The platform was assigned; the brand was your choice. Tell us who is in your team and which brand you picked in your platform's thread in the Slack channel #digitalmedia-flourishing-2026.

sections.heading: The three brands
sections.text: The briefs are vague on purpose so that you can be creative. The toilet paper can be fancy or cheap and funny; the fisher can be rude or charming. The audience does not have to be in Bhutan or Japan: choose the audience, research what they like, and build the strategy from that.

brands.name: Brand A · Individual · The Fisher
brands.situation: A young person who left the city to become a fisher in the countryside, with no money, trying to make a living as a content creator.
facts: One person, one small boat, very early starts, fish to catch every day, and knows how to cook.
Become a monetisable influencer and make an income from content.
Up to you. City people who dream of leaving? People who cook? Fishing hobbyists? Pick them and research what they watch.

brands.name: Brand B · Team · AI Translation Tool
brands.situation: A software company whose tool gives real-time translation between English, Japanese and Dzongkha. You are the marketer, and you need to promote the company.
facts: A small team with a working app that nobody knows yet.
Get the tool known and used.

Up to you. Exchange students and host families? Tour guides and their guests? Hospitals and clinics? Businesses trading between Japan and Bhutan? Families with one grandparent who speaks one language? Or a market you find yourself.

brands.name: Brand C · Small brand · Toilet Paper
brands.situation: A second-generation family mill with a small staff, making unbleached, slightly organic toilet paper. Nobody knows it yet.
facts: A normal toilet paper from a family mill. Small team, a factory floor, maybe a van.
Get known and increase revenue as soon as possible.
Up to you. It could be fancy or cheap as fuck: flat-sharers, families, cafés and offices buying in bulk, or whoever you decide.

sections.heading: What your strategy needs
sections.text: Build it together in a shared doc. Five parts:

steps.title: How your profile looks on the platform
steps.text: Name, bio, picture, and what the first posts look like together.

steps.title: Your target audience
steps.text: Who you are talking to, and why they are on this platform.

steps.title: The brand image and your competitive strategy
steps.text: What people should feel about the brand, and how it stands apart from everyone else selling the same thing. Look at how similar brands do it.

steps.title: How you will keep the audience engaged
steps.text: Not just reach. How do people come back, follow, save and share? The ladder below shows what the feed rewards.

steps.title: Two or three example posts
steps.text: What they look like, and what you hope people do with them.

sections.heading: The engagement ladder
sections.text: From what is cheap for a stranger to what is expensive, and what the feed rewards. Decide which steps your strategy is aiming for.

image.alt: The engagement ladder: impression, watch time, like, save, share, comment, reply, follow, message
image.caption: Impression, watch time, like, save, share or send, comment, reply, follow, message. Cheap for the stranger on the left; expensive, and what the feed rewards, on the right.

sections.heading: Presenting
sections.text: Each team presents in class on Wednesday 4 November (Week 6). I did not want to constrain the format, so it can be a demo, slides, a presentation, or the example posts themselves. No submission beforehand: you will share your screen and present.
items: Post your team members, your brand and, if you have one, the link to your shared doc in your platform's Slack thread.

assignments.submit: No submission before class. Share your screen and present on Wednesday 4 November. If you want to keep your files somewhere, the Week 4 Drive folder is there for that.

assignments.title: Before class: a reading on how infants learn
assignments.linkText: Reading and questions for this session
assignments.intro: Dr. Gal Raz has set a reading before his session. Note your answers to the two questions before you read, then answer the three questions after.

reading.citation: Raz, G. & Saxe, R. (2020). Learning in Infancy Is Active, Endogenously Motivated, and Depends on the Prefrontal Cortices. Annual Review of Developmental Psychology, 2, 247–268.

skip: The social brain: evidence from adults
The social brain: evidence from infants
before: In their first year of life, would you say humans learn more by A) observing whatever happens to be around them, or B) by actively choosing what to engage with?
What do humans learn first, A) low-level perceptual concepts like color, shapes and movement or B) high-level concepts like social relationships and physical laws (like gravity, collision etc.)?
after: Were you convinced that infants' learning depends on active choice of attentional targets?
Do you agree with the claim that infants have distinct motivations when deciding what to look at?
Which evidence did you find most convincing? Which evidence left some open questions for you?
assignments.submit: Submit your answers before class on Wednesday 28 October.
